items.title: Automatic transition sync dispatch stops when chain depth exceeds 50; the pipeline fails with error code Transition:100017.
items.workaround: Refactor the workflow so automatic chains do not exceed the depth guard, insert intermediate human states, or split logic across transitions.

items.title: If a scheduled transition has no timer configuration, ScheduleTransitionsStep logs a warning and skips enqueueing that schedule (transition does not fire from scheduling).
items.workaround: Ensure every scheduled transition defines a timer evaluated by the timer service.

items.title: When dynamic workflow timeout mapping fails, the runtime falls back to the static ISO 8601 duration from workflow timeout configuration.
items.workaround: Fix or simplify the timeout mapping script; verify TimeoutMappingFallback logs during instance start.

items.title: If enqueueing or persisting the workflow timeout background job throws, the failure is logged but instance start continues without blocking.
items.workaround: Monitor WorkflowTimeoutSchedulingFailed logs and job infrastructure; retry or reconcile timeouts externally if needed.

items.title: When cancelling scheduled transition jobs for the leaving state fails, the pipeline logs ScheduledJobsCancellationFailed and continues the transition anyway.
items.workaround: Inspect cancellation/job-store failures; manually reconcile orphaned scheduled jobs if transitions completed despite cancellation errors.

items.title: Async (sync=false) transition jobs could fire while the enqueue-side distributed lock still held the same instance key; the job consumer failed with a lock conflict that was silently swallowed, losing the transition and stranding the instance in Busy status.
items.workaround: Retry the transition after the instance is recovered; upgrade to a fixed version where the enqueue lock is scoped with an :enqueue suffix and the job handler retries lock conflicts and faults the instance on exhaustion.

items.title: A second async transition request for the same instance and transition key while a job is already active is rejected with HTTP 409 Conflict.
items.workaround: Use idempotency keys, poll instance state, or wait for the in-flight job to finish before retrying.

items.title: Instance data appends reformat every number through int/double, so integers above 2^53 (including values that no longer fit int64) and decimals beyond ~15 significant digits are persisted with reduced precision — and the rewrite touches numbers the append never referenced.
items.workaround: Set WorkflowExecution:InstanceDataWrite:PreserveNumericPrecision=true to canonicalize numbers losslessly (int64 exact, decimal in plain notation; values beyond decimal's 28-29 significant digits are still rounded). Enabling it changes the content hash once per affected instance — for values that lost precision, for values currently written in exponent notation (0.00001 becomes 0.00001 instead of 1E-05) and for a negative zero with a fraction (-0.0 becomes 0) — costing one extra version row and one phantom diff there, with no data loss. Alternatively carry exact monetary values as strings in the schema.

items.title: The internal enqueue relay's event-to-payload copy omitted SubflowChainReserved, so with WorkflowExecution:DirectEnqueueContinuations=false (or when the direct Dapr enqueue falls back to the outbox) an async transition on a parent with an active SubFlow reached the leaf without the chain-reserve claim its own accept had taken, and the leaf rejected the forward as Busy (Instance:100031).
items.workaround: Keep DirectEnqueueContinuations=true (the default); the drop then only bites when the direct Dapr enqueue fails and the outbox fallback carries a subflow-forward transition. Retrying the transition after the fallback window is the only recovery on affected versions.

items.title: The Aether arming poller is registered only by the Orchestration host and switched off there (WithHostedService=false, also in the vnext-runtime deployment templates), so no process arms recovery. When the immediate Dapr scheduler arm fails (scheduler restart/outage at accept, timer arm, ack-timeout arm), Aether rolls the job row back to Pending 'for the arming poller' - and nothing ever arms it. The async accept has already answered 202 and reserved the instance, so the instance stays Busy forever; retries are rejected by the Busy check and the duplicate-active-job guard. Verified live (issue #935 chaos test): a Pending row sat unarmed for 15 minutes with the scheduler healthy again; enabling the poller recovered it within seconds.
items.workaround: Set BackgroundJob:WithHostedService=true on exactly one host (orchestration) so the arming poller and reapers run. A stuck instance can be recovered manually by setting its sys_queues.BackgroundJobs row Status back to 5 (Pending) with the poller enabled.

items.title: Arming a past-due one-shot races the Dapr scheduler's immediate fire: the job callback can arrive before the armer commits Pending->Scheduled, JobDispatcher answers 'not found in an active state; skipping' with HTTP 200, Dapr deletes the consumed one-shot, and the armer then commits Scheduled - leaving a Scheduled row with no scheduler entry, permanently. The VisibilityTimeout reaper covers Running rows only, so nothing recovers it. Observed live (issue #935 chaos test, outbox mode + poller on): dispatcher skip at 12:17:38Z, row Scheduled for 11+ minutes, instance Busy. Aether-level defect; the same orphan also results from a failed rollback after a direct-arm timeout whose server-side registration succeeded.
items.workaround: Manual: set the orphaned sys_queues.BackgroundJobs row Status back to 5 (Pending) so the poller re-arms it (Dapr one-shot arming is overwrite-idempotent). No configuration prevents the race.

items.title: The registry's domain-list function serves a single page (500 rows today) and its response carries no truncation signal, so a registry holding more domains than that warms only the first 500.
items.workaround: The runtime logs WorkflowLogs 50038 DomainListCeilingReached at Warning when the list comes back at or above ServiceDiscovery:Cache:DomainListExpectedMax, and publishes it anyway - the domains beyond the ceiling are simply not warmed and each pays a live per-domain lookup, which is the behaviour with the cache switched off. Raising the ceiling is a change on the registry side (vnext-domain-discovery, DomainListMapping.csx pageSize).

items.title: timer.reset is required by the schema but is read NOWHERE in the runtime, so a workflow timeout always means 'not finished within duration, counted from instance start' and never 'idle for duration'. Whatever the field says - 'never', 'OnEntry' - the behaviour is identical.
items.workaround: Author the duration as an absolute budget from start and do not rely on activity resetting it; every authored value in the reference corpus today declares OnEntry against a runtime that ignores it. The instant is resolved once when the scheduler is armed (mapping script included) and never re-armed, which is also why the state function's timeout.executeAtUtc is stable for the instance's whole life. Expressing an idle timeout needs a per-state scheduled transition (triggerType 2), which IS cancelled and re-armed on every state entry.

items.title: A state starts a SubFlow and only a SubFlow: state.subFlow.type must be 'S'. A SubProcess is started by its own task (SubProcessTask, TaskType.SubProcess = 14), which creates the correlation itself, not by a state. WorkflowValidator now rejects a state-level subFlow.type of 'P' at publish. This is not a regression: the shape never worked on the sync path - it returned 409 Instance:100031 and left the parent Busy and not Faulted with no automatic recovery - and only appeared to work when driven asynchronously, where a job re-entry happened to carry IsPreReserved.
items.workaround: Model the SubProcess as a SubProcessTask on a transition or state hook instead of as state.subFlow, keeping the child workflow itself unchanged.

items.title: An async accept flips Busy before answering 202, and a job re-entry that fails with a non-lock-conflict Result error (for example a policy re-validation failure) logs JobFailed and returns without faulting, so that Busy can be left with no owner - the pipeline's own fault path covers only failures inside the step loop, retry requires Faulted, and the sync path leaves no job row for recovery. Note that a blanket "fault on any job failure" is not the fix: it faults a parent that is legitimately Busy for its subflow child's lifetime, which was measured to break a working chain (ChainBusy.PostCommitForwardFailure_ReleasesTheChainReserve_SoNoLevelStaysBusy, root left Faulted in root-waiting with a JOB_EXECUTION_FAILED incident). A correct fix needs a predicate for "this execution owns that Busy", which the job handler does not have today.
items.workaround: Recover a stranded instance manually with cancel/exit; prefer sync for transitions whose policy may change between accept and re-entry.

items.title: In a function with multiple onExecutionTasks, every ScriptContext.TaskResponse slot carried the LAST executed task's payload: SetStandardResponse aliased each response tree into the shared Body, and the in-place expando merge of the next task's response rewrote the earlier slots. Output scripts reading TaskResponse composed the wrong response; OutputResponse slots (re-serialized snapshots) were unaffected.
items.workaround: Read task results from ScriptContext.OutputResponse[variableName] instead of TaskResponse, or publish the function with a single task. Fixed in 0.0.95 (#1025): TaskResponse slots are isolated per task and duplicate normalized task keys are rejected at publish.

items.title: Re-publishing a master schema at the same version with changed x-masking (or x-roles) does not move the data-function ETag; clients holding a body keep it (304) until the instance data changes or the cache entry expires.
items.workaround: Bump the schema version whenever x-masking or x-roles changes. A schema-generation token in the ETag material is the candidate fix, pending a 304-path latency measurement.

items.title: Instance list filters, sorting and groupBy run on the raw JSONB value, so a caller can probe an x-roles-hidden field through them. x-masking cannot be combined with x-filterOperators/x-sortable (rejected at publish), but the x-roles case is pre-existing.
items.workaround: Do not declare x-filterOperators or x-sortable on fields guarded by x-roles; set Workflow:InstanceFiltering:EnforceMasterSchemaFiltering=true so only declared fields are filterable.

items.title: x-encryption hash is pseudonymisation, not anonymisation: low-entropy values (national ids, phone numbers) can be brute-forced by anyone who can read the instance's salt from InstanceSecrets.
items.workaround: Restrict database access; use x-roles to hide values that must not be matchable at all.

items.title: x-encryption 'encrypt' covers InstancesData only: InstanceTransition.Body/Header, InstanceTask.Request/Response/InvocationResult, outbox InstanceSubCompleted/Faulted payloads, job payloads and the human-task cache still hold the plaintext
items.workaround: Treat encrypt as InstanceData field encryption, not 'PII encrypted at rest'. Restrict database/backup access accordingly; Phase 2 extends encryption to these copies.

items.title: Rows written before a field became x-encryption 'encrypt' stay plaintext (append-only history, lazy migration); new rows are encrypted
items.workaround: A backfill tool is Phase 2. Until then treat history rows written before enablement as plaintext.

items.title: The per-instance x-encryption key and salt are stored in plaintext in the flow schema's InstanceSecrets table next to the data they protect; a database reader (or a script with raw database access) can decrypt every encrypt value
items.workaround: Accepted (requester decision): database security is owned by the DB team and the runtime never serves the secrets. encrypt protects API exposure and single-table dumps, not a database reader.

items.title: A runtime older than 0.0.99 cannot open x-encryption tokens and would hand them to the engine as values
items.workaround: Publish the first encrypt/hash schema only after every orchestration pod runs >= 0.0.99 and its migration (InstanceSecrets) is applied; roll back with SchemaEncryption__EncryptWrites=false rather than a binary downgrade.

items.title: Event selectors (FindByFilterAsync) carry no schema context and are not refused on an x-encryption 'encrypt' path; they match ciphertext and silently find nothing
items.workaround: Never select on an encrypted field in an event mapping or selector.

items.title: x-encryption tokens are bound to scheme, instance and path but not to the row, so a database writer could swap tokens between versions of the same instance and path without detection
items.workaround: Accepted: it keeps unchanged values' tokens stable, echo possible and rollback safe. Database write access is outside the threat model.

items.title: A write that would carry an unopenable x-encryption encrypt value forward (its InstanceSecrets row deleted outside the runtime, or the token tampered) is refused with Instance:100040 at the write, so the transition fails at the step that writes instead of being refused before admission; reads keep serving the token
items.workaround: The runtime deletes a secret row only together with its instance. A missing row is crypto-shredded data: cancel the instance, or write a new value to the field.

items.title: x-encryption hash digests use a per-instance salt, so the same value hashes differently in two instances; digests cannot be joined or deduplicated across instances
items.workaround: By design. Keep a value that must be matched across instances outside hash (e.g. under x-roles).

items.title: Deleting an instance's InstanceSecrets row (crypto-shredding) takes effect on a pod only once its in-process L1 entry is gone (sliding SchemaEncryption:SecretCacheSlidingMinutes, default 30, or a restart); until then that pod keeps opening the values
items.workaround: After shredding, wait out the sliding window or restart the orchestration pods.

items.title: CacheAsideTask ran its source task without the source mapping's InputHandler: sourceMapping was applied only as output shaping over the cached raw source result, so a source that needs its configuration set by a mapping (for example GetInstanceData SetKey, an HTTP URL or body) ran unconfigured, and the cache held the raw payload instead of the shaped value.
items.workaround: Upgrade to 0.0.98, where the source runs as a task with sourceMapping as its mapping (InputHandler -> invoke -> OutputHandler) and the shaped output is cached. Until then, run the configuring task separately in onExecutionTasks.

items.title: Task invokers treated X-Request-Id as a reserved trace header: a value set in the task's headers or input mapping was silently dropped from the outbound call and no value was sent in its place, so APIs that require it (OHVPS/BKM) rejected the call with 400 TR.OHVPS.Resource.InvalidFormat. StartTrigger and SubProcess never dropped the mapping's value but did not send vNext's request id either.
items.workaround: Upgrade to 0.0.98, where a non-empty X-Request-Id from the input mapping is sent as is and, when the mapping sets none, vNext's own request id (the originating request's X-Request-Id) is sent — on every HTTP-shaped task type, StartTrigger and SubProcess included. Until then, call such APIs through a proxy that adds the header.

items.path: roles[] | queryRoles[] | transitions[].roles[] | availableIn[].roles[] | schema x-roles[] | subFlow.overrides (allOf / anyOf grants)
items.title: A runtime older than 0.0.99 cannot read an allOf / anyOf grant: the flow fails to load, a combinator override stamp is treated as malformed (the child falls back to its own grants), and an old x-roles parser skips the entry so a combinator deny vanishes
items.workaround: Author the first allOf / anyOf grant only after every pod, and every domain that stamps overrides onto this one, runs a release containing combinators. Do not binary-downgrade once a combinator has been published: remove the combinator grants (or re-publish without them) first.
